# On the Reliability of Generated Answers: A Study on TriviaCheck

## Abstract

Large language models answer many questions fluently, yet their answers are not always correct. We compare the closed-book model with the retrieval-augmented generator on TriviaCheck. Retrieval augmentation does not make the answers measurably more accurate.

## Introduction

Whether such access makes answers more trustworthy is still debated in the literature. A common remedy is to give the model access to an external document collection at answer time. We release our prompts and evaluation scripts to support replication. Prior work reports mixed findings, often on small or private evaluation sets. Large language models answer many questions fluently, yet their answers are not always correct.

## Method

We evaluate on TriviaCheck, a benchmark of 1,000 questions with reference answers. We include the closed-book model, which answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. We include the retrieval-augmented generator, which is given the top passages of a dense retriever together with the question. We include the RAG without reranking, which uses the same retriever but keeps the passages in their original order. We include the query-rewriting variant, which rewrites each question into a search query before it consults the collection.

Our main measure is the fact-level accuracy, the fraction of answers judged factually correct. Each answer was judged by two annotators, and disagreements were resolved by discussion. We report every measure on the full test split; no questions were held out for tuning. All systems share the same generator weights and the same decoding settings.

## Results

We measure 56.4% fact-level accuracy for the closed-book model on TriviaCheck. On TriviaCheck, the retrieval-augmented generator has 57.2% fact-level accuracy. The RAG without reranking shows 72.3% fact-level accuracy on TriviaCheck. On TriviaCheck, the query-rewriting variant has 58.9% fact-level accuracy.

## Discussion

Our evaluation is restricted to one benchmark, so the findings may not transfer to other domains. Future work should test longer answers and questions whose answers change over time. Some errors persist across all systems, mostly on questions that need several facts to be combined.

## Conclusion

Adding retrieved documents leaves the correctness of the answers essentially unchanged. Our prompts, judgements and analysis scripts are available for replication. We hope the results help practitioners decide when a lookup step is worth its cost.

# Research protocol for the first question (supervisor's design, 14 Oct 2026); protocol version 2 (17 Oct):
# the synthesis rules and the screening question are declared here (docs/evidence-system.md Part C).
# Written by hand before any run; the engine runs it as it stands. Its sha256 is the digest of the parsed
# content (evidence/protocol.py), so comments and layout do not change it.

id: rag-factuality
version: 2
question: Does retrieval-augmented generation improve the factual accuracy of LLM-generated answers?

locate:
  strategy: exhaustive        # exhaustive | bm25 | agent
  params:
    chunk_chars: 1500         # bm25: size of the ranked passages
    top_k: 6                  # bm25: passages kept per document and evidence type

screen:                       # per document, before any extraction (the funnel engine, Part D)
  question: >-
    Does the paper report an experiment that compares a retrieval-augmented system with the same model
    answering without retrieval?
  terms: [retrieval-augmented, retrieval augmented, RAG, retrieval, closed-book, without retrieval]
  extractors:
    - name: regex_screen      # no term in the paper: not relevant
    - name: llm_screen        # otherwise the model answers the question
  on_fail: skip               # skip | extract_anyway

evidence_types:
  condition:
    description: >-
      An experimental condition the paper compares: a system variant whose results are reported. role is
      rag for the retrieval-augmented system, baseline for the same model answering without retrieval
      (closed-book), other for anything else (ablations, other systems).
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [label, role]
      properties:
        label: {type: string, minLength: 1, description: the condition's name as the paper gives it}
        role: {type: string, enum: [rag, baseline, other], description: "rag, baseline or other"}
    roles: [condition_label]
    merge_key: [label, role]
    query: [retrieval, augmented, RAG, closed-book, baseline, without, variant, system, condition, compare]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_condition
      - name: llm_condition

  metric:
    description: >-
      An evaluation metric the paper reports results on. canonical is factual_accuracy for accuracy of the
      answers (accuracy, exact match, factual accuracy), hallucination_rate for the rate of hallucinated or
      unsupported answers, other for anything else (latency, BLEU, fluency).
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [name, canonical, higher_is_better]
      properties:
        name: {type: string, minLength: 1, description: the metric's name as the paper gives it}
        canonical: {type: string, enum: [factual_accuracy, hallucination_rate, other]}
        higher_is_better: {type: boolean}
    roles: [metric_label]
    merge_key: [name, canonical]
    query: [accuracy, factual, hallucination, rate, metric, measure, evaluate, score, exact, match]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_metric
      - name: llm_metric

  measurement:
    description: >-
      One reported result: the value of one metric for one condition. value is normalised to a fraction
      (62% and 62.0 under a % header are 0.62). dataset is the dataset it was measured on, or null.
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [value, dataset]
      properties:
        value: {type: number, description: the value as a fraction for accuracies and rates}
        dataset: {type: [string, "null"], description: "the dataset, or null when the paper does not say"}
    links: {condition: condition, metric: metric}
    bounds:                   # accuracies and rates are fractions; a value outside [0, 1] is rejected (schema)
      - {field: value, min: 0, max: 1, when: {link: metric, field: canonical, values: [factual_accuracy, hallucination_rate]}}
    context: [condition, metric]
    roles: [value, condition_label, metric_label]
    merge_key: [value]
    query: [table, results, accuracy, rate, achieves, reaches, compared, "%"]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_measurement
      - name: llm_measurement

  author_claim:
    description: >-
      The authors' own conclusion about whether retrieval augmentation improves the factual accuracy of
      the answers: improves, no_effect or worsens.
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [direction]
      properties:
        direction: {type: string, enum: [improves, no_effect, worsens]}
    roles: [claim]
    query: [conclusion, improves, show, find, retrieval, hurts, effect, accuracy]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_author_claim
      - name: llm_author_claim

synthesis:                    # every rule parameter; the machinery is evidence/rules.py and evidence/synthesis.py
  compare: {treatment: rag, control: baseline}   # condition roles a study's pair is made of
  metrics:                    # question metrics in priority order; the first one with a usable pair decides
    - {canonical: factual_accuracy, higher_is_better: true}
    - {canonical: hallucination_rate, higher_is_better: false}
  min_effect: 0.01            # |delta| below this (fractions) is neutral
  pairing:                    # treatment and control on the same dataset (first dataset in document order
    rule: same_dataset        # that has both); among several values of one condition, metric and dataset
    prefer: [table_cell, document_order]   # a table cell beats prose, then the earlier value wins
  claim_map: {improves: supports, worsens: contradicts, no_effect: neutral}   # author claim -> direction it asserts
  label:                      # the answer from the counts: the first row whose conditions all hold
    - {when: {supporting: ">0", contradicting: ">0"}, then: mixed}
    - {when: {supporting: ">0"}, then: supported}
    - {when: {contradicting: ">0"}, then: refuted}
    - {when: {neutral: ">0"}, then: no_effect}
    - {then: insufficient}
  flags:                      # reported in answer.json (Part F); only duplicates change the counts
    duplicates: true
    large_effect: {factor: 3.0, min_studies: 3}

# Research protocol for the first question (supervisor's design, 14 Oct 2026); protocol version 2 (17 Oct):
# the synthesis rules and the screening question are declared here (docs/evidence-system.md Part C).
# Written by hand before any run; the engine runs it as it stands. Its sha256 is the digest of the parsed
# content (evidence/protocol.py), so comments and layout do not change it.

id: rag-factuality
version: 2
question: Does retrieval-augmented generation improve the factual accuracy of LLM-generated answers?

locate:
  strategy: exhaustive        # exhaustive | bm25 | agent
  params:
    chunk_chars: 1500         # bm25: size of the ranked passages
    top_k: 6                  # bm25: passages kept per document and evidence type

screen:                       # per document, before any extraction (the funnel engine, Part D)
  question: >-
    Does the paper report an experiment that compares a retrieval-augmented system with the same model
    answering without retrieval?
  terms: [retrieval-augmented, retrieval augmented, RAG, retrieval, closed-book, without retrieval]
  extractors:
    - name: regex_screen      # no term in the paper: not relevant
    - name: llm_screen        # otherwise the model answers the question
  on_fail: skip               # skip | extract_anyway

evidence_types:
  condition:
    description: >-
      An experimental condition the paper compares: a system variant whose results are reported. role is
      rag for the retrieval-augmented system, baseline for the same model answering without retrieval
      (closed-book), other for anything else (ablations, other systems).
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [label, role]
      properties:
        label: {type: string, minLength: 1, description: the condition's name as the paper gives it}
        role: {type: string, enum: [rag, baseline, other], description: "rag, baseline or other"}
    roles: [condition_label]
    merge_key: [label, role]
    query: [retrieval, augmented, RAG, closed-book, baseline, without, variant, system, condition, compare]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_condition
      - name: llm_condition

  metric:
    description: >-
      An evaluation metric the paper reports results on. canonical is factual_accuracy for accuracy of the
      answers (accuracy, exact match, factual accuracy), hallucination_rate for the rate of hallucinated or
      unsupported answers, other for anything else (latency, BLEU, fluency).
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [name, canonical, higher_is_better]
      properties:
        name: {type: string, minLength: 1, description: the metric's name as the paper gives it}
        canonical: {type: string, enum: [factual_accuracy, hallucination_rate, other]}
        higher_is_better: {type: boolean}
    roles: [metric_label]
    merge_key: [name, canonical]
    query: [accuracy, factual, hallucination, rate, metric, measure, evaluate, score, exact, match]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_metric
      - name: llm_metric

  measurement:
    description: >-
      One reported result: the value of one metric for one condition. value is normalised to a fraction
      (62% and 62.0 under a % header are 0.62). dataset is the dataset it was measured on, or null.
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [value, dataset]
      properties:
        value: {type: number, description: the value as a fraction for accuracies and rates}
        dataset: {type: [string, "null"], description: "the dataset, or null when the paper does not say"}
    links: {condition: condition, metric: metric}
    bounds:                   # accuracies and rates are fractions; a value outside [0, 1] is rejected (schema)
      - {field: value, min: 0, max: 1, when: {link: metric, field: canonical, values: [factual_accuracy, hallucination_rate]}}
    context: [condition, metric]
    roles: [value, condition_label, metric_label]
    merge_key: [value]
    query: [table, results, accuracy, rate, achieves, reaches, compared, "%"]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_measurement
      - name: llm_measurement

  author_claim:
    description: >-
      The authors' own conclusion about whether retrieval augmentation improves the factual accuracy of
      the answers: improves, no_effect or worsens.
    fields:
      type: object
      additionalProperties: false
      required: [direction]
      properties:
        direction: {type: string, enum: [improves, no_effect, worsens]}
    roles: [claim]
    query: [conclusion, improves, show, find, retrieval, hurts, effect, accuracy]
    extractors:
      - name: regex_author_claim
      - name: llm_author_claim

synthesis:                    # every rule parameter; the machinery is evidence/rules.py and evidence/synthesis.py
  compare: {treatment: rag, control: baseline}   # condition roles a study's pair is made of
  metrics:                    # question metrics in priority order; the first one with a usable pair decides
    - {canonical: factual_accuracy, higher_is_better: true}

# On the Reliability of Generated Answers: A Study on TriviaCheck

## Abstract

Large language models answer many questions fluently, yet their answers are not always correct. We compare the closed-book model with the retrieval-augmented generator on TriviaCheck. Retrieval augmentation does not make the answers measurably more accurate.

## Introduction

Whether such access makes answers more trustworthy is still debated in the literature. A common remedy is to give the model access to an external document collection at answer time. We release our prompts and evaluation scripts to support replication. Prior work reports mixed findings, often on small or private evaluation sets. Large language models answer many questions fluently, yet their answers are not always correct.

## Method

We evaluate on TriviaCheck, a benchmark of 1,000 questions with reference answers. We include the closed-book model, which answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. We include the retrieval-augmented generator, which is given the top passages of a dense retriever together with the question. We include the RAG without reranking, which uses the same retriever but keeps the passages in their original order. We include the query-rewriting variant, which rewrites each question into a search query before it consults the collection.

Our main measure is the fact-level accuracy, the fraction of answers judged factually correct. Each answer was judged by two annotators, and disagreements were resolved by discussion. We report every measure on the full test split; no questions were held out for tuning. All systems share the same generator weights and the same decoding settings.

## Results

We measure 56.4% fact-level accuracy for the closed-book model on TriviaCheck. On TriviaCheck, the retrieval-augmented generator has 57.2% fact-level accuracy. The RAG without reranking shows 72.3% fact-level accuracy on TriviaCheck. On TriviaCheck, the query-rewriting variant has 58.9% fact-level accuracy.

## Discussion

Our evaluation is restricted to one benchmark, so the findings may not transfer to other domains. Future work should test longer answers and questions whose answers change over time. Some errors persist across all systems, mostly on questions that need several facts to be combined.

## Conclusion

Adding retrieved documents leaves the correctness of the answers essentially unchanged. Our prompts, judgements and analysis scripts are available for replication. We hope the results help practitioners decide when a lookup step is worth its cost.

# Looking It Up: Retrieval and Factuality in Open-Domain Answers on PopCultureQA

## Abstract

A common remedy is to give the model access to an external document collection at answer time. We compare the closed-book model with the retrieval-augmented model on PopCultureQA. Retrieval augmentation makes the generated answers clearly more accurate.

## Introduction

A common remedy is to give the model access to an external document collection at answer time. Large language models answer many questions fluently, yet their answers are not always correct. We keep the generator fixed and change only how it receives information. Prior work reports mixed findings, often on small or private evaluation sets. Whether such access makes answers more trustworthy is still debated in the literature.

## Method

We evaluate on PopCultureQA, a benchmark of 1,000 questions with reference answers. We include the closed-book model, which answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. We include the retrieval-augmented model, which retrieves passages from the reference collection and conditions its answer on them.

Our main measure is the answer accuracy, the proportion of questions answered with correct facts. Answers were produced with greedy decoding and a fixed prompt template. Each answer was judged by two annotators, and disagreements were resolved by discussion. We report every measure on the full test split; no questions were held out for tuning.

## Results

We measure 53.5% answer accuracy for the closed-book model on PopCultureQA. On PopCultureQA, the retrieval-augmented model has 60.3% answer accuracy.

## Discussion

Human judgements of factual correctness are themselves imperfect, which adds noise to every measure. Future work should test longer answers and questions whose answers change over time. Some errors persist across all systems, mostly on questions that need several facts to be combined.

## Conclusion

Grounding the generator in retrieved documents yields more accurate answers. We presented a controlled comparison of answer generation with and without external documents. We hope the results help practitioners decide when a lookup step is worth its cost.
